meta.subtitle: A wide-moat derivatives exchange with low, steady leverage, priced near fair value as second-quarter volumes cool

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 62pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary: CME Group runs the futures and options exchanges of CME, CBOT, NYMEX and COMEX and the clearing house behind them, and it turns that position into exceptional economics: a 64.9% operating margin in FY25, $83.5M of capital expenditure against $4.3B of operating cash flow, and $3.9B of dividends paid out of $4.2B of free cash flow. The re-captured balance sheet corrects one part of the earlier picture. CME has carried $3.4B of debt in each of the last five years, so it was a small net debtor from FY21 through FY24, held net cash of about $1.0B only at the FY25 year-end, and was back to net debt by June 30, 2026. Leverage is low, not absent: net debt/EBITDA reads 0.3x on a trailing basis. The second quarter is the reason for caution. Total revenue rose 1%, clearing and transaction fees fell 3% and the average rate per contract fell 2% as, in the company's account, market volatility subsided after a very volatile start to the year. At $276.01 the shares trade at 23.4x trailing earnings and about 21.4x FY27E, with a split Street (7 Buy, 6 Hold, 3 Sell) and a $283.60 consensus target. We rate CME HOLD with a $250-$300 target range. Our Base of $285.00 is the Street's median target, which on FY27E EPS of $12.93 means a slightly lower forward multiple a year out as growth slows to the mid-single digits. The Bull ($330.00) and Bear ($230.00) sit at the ends of the Street's target range, each argued on its own earnings and multiple. Weighted 20/55/25, the scenarios give a fair value of $280.25 and an expected upside of 1.5% against a bear-case downside of 16.7%. The franchise is not in question; the price already pays for it, and near-term earnings follow market volatility the company does not control.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: CME Group, founded in 1898 and headquartered in Chicago, operates contract markets for futures and options on interest rates, equity indexes, foreign exchange, energy, agricultural commodities and metals, and runs the clearing house that clears, settles and guarantees those contracts. It also runs cash markets in fixed income through BrokerTec and in foreign exchange through EBS. The company was known as Chicago Mercantile Exchange Holdings Inc. until July 2007. Revenue comes in three lines: clearing and transaction fees, which follow trading volume; market data and information services; and other. FY25 revenue was $6.5B at a 64.9% operating margin, with net income of $4.1B and diluted EPS of $11.16. The company reports a single segment. It bills a substantial portion of its clearing and transaction fees to clearing firms, and one firm represented at least 10% of those fees in the first six months of 2026. The business needs little capital, carries a fixed block of long-term debt, and returns most of its cash to shareholders. The one input the model cannot set is trading volume, and the second quarter of 2026 is where that showed.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: CME pairs a wide moat with a price that already reflects it, and the swing factor between the two is trading volume, which the company does not control. The liquidity in its benchmark contracts and the margin offsets of clearing them at one house keep customers in place, and the cost base is light enough that most revenue reaches shareholders. The second quarter showed the other side: volume and clearing fees slipped as volatility subsided, and consensus for FY26 needs a second-half pickup the quarter did not show. Our Base assumes consensus earnings and a slightly lower forward multiple a year out, which lands on the Street's median target. The Bull needs the volatility of early 2026 to return; the Bear needs the second quarter's conditions to persist into 2027. The balance sheet is not the debate: debt has been steady for five years and leverage is low. We hold because the weighted value sits within a few percent of the price.

catalysts: A return of the volatility behind the record first-quarter trading the company reported would lift volume, the line revenue is most geared to.
Market data keeps growing faster than the trading business, a stream that does not depend on volume; the growth section takes it up.
New products the company lists, including Single-Stock futures, 1-Ounce Gold contracts and U.S. Treasury clearing, are optional upside not yet visible in the figures.
Capital return continues through dividends and buybacks, as the cash-flow discussion sets out.
risks: Volume dependence: revenue follows market volatility, and the second quarter showed volume and clearing fees falling as volatility subsided.
Rate per contract: growth in lower-priced micro contracts and in member trading lowered the average fee in the quarter.
Valuation: with a consensus target 2.7% above the price, the shares carry little margin of safety.
Regulation: the 10-K flags a possible transaction tax and rules that could require more funds for the guaranty fund.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue grew from $4.7B in FY21 to $6.5B in FY25, up 6.4% in the latest year, while operating income rose from $2.6B to $4.2B and diluted EPS from $7.29 to $11.16. The operating margin widened from 56.4% to 64.9% over the period because costs grew more slowly than revenue. An exchange has no cost of goods, so the gross-margin line is blank and operating margin carries the profitability read. The second quarter of 2026 is the cleaner read on the current run-rate. Total revenue of $1,706.2 million was up 1% year over year: clearing and transaction fees fell 3% to $1,352.5 million, market data and information services rose 20% to $238.1 million, and other revenue rose 9%. The average rate per contract fell to $0.678 from $0.690. Total expenses rose 6%, with technology at $83.3 million against $70.9 million and licensing and other fee agreements at $109.1 million against $96.2 million, so the quarter's operating margin fell from 66.7% a year earlier to the same level as the FY25 full-year margin. Below the operating line, non-operating income was $220.6 million, up 10%; it nets $1,429.7 million of investment income against $1,263.2 million of other non-operating expense and adds $97.7 million of equity in the earnings of unconsolidated subsidiaries. A lower effective tax rate, 21.5% against 22.9%, helped net income rise 2% to $1,041.8 million and diluted EPS to $2.88 from $2.81. The first half looks stronger because of the first quarter: six-month revenue rose 8%, diluted EPS rose 12% to $6.06 and the operating margin was 67.4%. We read the second quarter, with costs rising faster than revenue, as the better guide to the coming quarters.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: CME carries a steady block of debt. Total debt was $3.4B in every year from FY21 to FY25, and long-term debt was $3,424.2 million at June 30, 2026. Against it, cash and short-term investments ran between $2.8B and $3.0B in FY21 to FY24, leaving net debt of $0.5B to $0.7B, before rising to $4.5B in FY25 and leaving net cash of about $1.0B at that year-end. The net-cash position did not last. Cash and cash equivalents fell from $4,416.9 million at December 31, 2025 to $2,144.2 million at June 30, 2026. The earnings release puts cash at $2.3 billion, a broader figure that includes $200 million deposited with Fixed Income Clearing Corporation and held in other current assets; we use the release figure, which it sets against $3.4 billion of debt. On a trailing basis net debt/EBITDA reads 0.3x, a low but real figure. The pack leaves interest coverage blank; the income statement shows $43.6 million of interest and other borrowing costs in the second quarter against $1,107.1 million of operating income, so servicing the debt is not a constraint. The balance sheet also carries $158,110.7 million of performance bonds and guaranty fund contributions on both sides, which is why the current ratio sits near 1.0 (1.02 on a trailing basis); that collateral is posted by clearing members and is not CME's own capital. Shareholders' equity of $26,520.4 million at June 30, 2026 is smaller than the $17,175.3 million of trading-product intangibles and $10,505.8 million of goodwill combined, so book value says little about the economics. Leverage is low and stable, and the swing between net debt and net cash reflects how much cash the company is holding before it pays it out, not new borrowing.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow rose from $2.4B in FY21 to $4.3B in FY25, and free cash flow tracked it, reaching $4.2B in FY25 at a 64.3% FCF margin, because capital expenditure was only $83.5M in FY25. Dividends paid rose every year, from $2.2B in FY21 to $3.9B in FY25, so the company paid out most of each year's free cash flow as dividends. The vendor table shows no share-repurchase line, while the earnings release reports $695 million of repurchases and about $468 million of dividends in the second quarter of 2026; we use the release. First-half 2026 operating cash flow was $2,207.0 million, up 1%. Distributions in the first half ran well ahead of earnings: shareholders' equity fell from $28,728.2 million at December 31, 2025 to the June 30 level noted above despite $2,196.1 million of first-half net income, and that drawdown is what took the balance sheet from net cash back to net debt. The pack itemizes only the second quarter's dividends and buybacks. The policy is coherent for a business that needs little reinvestment: the debt stays fixed and the surplus goes out. The cost is a thinner cash cushion than at the FY25 year-end, which matters only if volume and cash generation fall together.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $276.01 CME trades at 23.4x trailing earnings, 14.7x sales and 22.2x EV/EBITDA on a trailing basis. With $3.4B of debt now captured, the enterprise-value multiple is meaningful, and it sits close to the P/E because net debt is small next to a market capitalization of about $99.2B. Two forward multiples appear in the pack. The snapshot shows about 21.4x on FY27E EPS of $12.93; the multiples block shows 22.5x labelled NTM, which lines up with the FY26E estimate of $12.25, so we read it as a current-year multiple. When we value the shares a year out on FY27E earnings, the like-for-like reference is that NTM multiple. The dividend yield is 1.88% and the trailing FCF yield 4.2%. The Street is divided: 16 analysts split Buy 7, Hold 6 and Sell 3 for a consensus Hold, with a consensus target of $283.60, a median of $285.00 and a range of $230.00-$330.00. The price sits near the middle of a 52-week range of $218.31-$329.16, well below the high, and the width of that range shows how far the shares have moved within a year. No peer column exists in this pack, so the multiples are judged against CME's own earnings path rather than against other exchanges. On that path, the multiples are full but not stretched for a franchise growing earnings at the mid-single-digit pace FY27E consensus implies.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Volatility returns at something like the early-2026 level, when the company reported record first-quarter trading. Volume and market data run ahead of plan and EPS beats the FY27E consensus. The top of the Street's target range, $330.00, next to the 52-week high of $329.16, is above 23.4x on consensus FY27E EPS, so this case needs both an earnings beat and a multiple richer than today's trailing one. The shares traded near that level within the past year.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Volume stays near second-quarter levels with normal swings, market data keeps growing, and EPS reaches consensus of $12.25 for FY26E and $12.93 for FY27E. A year out the forward multiple slips slightly below today's 22.5x as growth slows to the mid-single digits. That lands on the Street's median target of $285.00. Holding today's forward multiple on FY27E EPS would put the Base a little higher, and it would not change the label.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The second quarter's conditions persist into 2027: volatility stays low, interest-rate and energy volume keep falling, and micro-contract growth keeps pulling the rate per contract down. EPS falls short of the FY26E consensus, FY27E growth stalls, and the multiple falls well below today's 21.4x FY27E multiple as investors stop paying for growth. The price reaches the bottom of the Street's target range, $230.00, still above the 52-week low of $218.31.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: All three scenarios use one framework: a P/E on the FY26E-FY27E earnings path, with each price set at a Street target a reader can check and argued on its own earnings and multiple. We weight the Base at 55% because consensus already builds in slower growth for FY27E, and the first half's 12% EPS gain gives FY26E some cushion even if the second quarter's pace persists. The Bear gets 25% against the Bull's 20%. The second quarter looks more like the Bear's starting point than the Bull's, and the Bull needs both an earnings beat and a higher multiple. The tilt is small because volatility is two-sided, and the first quarter showed how quickly it can return. The scenarios give a weighted fair value of $280.25, an expected upside of 1.5% and a bear-case downside of 16.7%, for a reward/risk of 0.09x. That is a HOLD, and it is not close. Swapping the Bull and Bear weights still derives HOLD, and so does holding today's forward multiple in the Base. Reaching SELL would take a much heavier Bear weight or a Base well below the Street's median. The $250-$300 target range brackets the Base.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: CME reports a single segment, but its product complexes moved in different directions in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate average daily volume fell 1% to 29,843 thousand contracts. Interest rates, at 14,532 thousand contracts a day, fell 6% and energy fell 13%, which the company tied to more certainty about Federal Reserve policy and to price stabilization in energy. Equity indexes rose by as much as energy fell and agricultural commodities also gained, while foreign exchange fell 10% and metals were flat. Electronic trading was 94% of volume. The single segment therefore hides real diversification: no one complex decides the result, though interest rates carry more volume than any other complex, and a soft quarter in rates and energy was partly cushioned by gains elsewhere.

moatFactors.name: Liquidity network effect
moatFactors.body: A futures market is useful only if it is liquid, and liquidity draws more of itself. The 10-K describes the reverse loop: a reduction in trading volume could make its markets less attractive as a source of liquidity, which could lead to a further loss of volume. The same loop protects the incumbent. A competitor must win liquidity before it can win trades, and CME's benchmark products across all major asset classes give it that position across the board.

moatFactors.name: Cross-margined clearing
moatFactors.body: CME clears what it trades, and clearing correlated positions at one house lets participants offset margin. The company says it provided more than $95 billion in daily margin efficiencies in the second quarter of 2026. A participant who moves one product elsewhere gives up part of that saving, which makes open interest sticky in a way a trading venue alone could not achieve.

moatFactors.name: Regulatory status
moatFactors.body: CME's exchanges and clearing house operate as designated contract markets and a derivatives clearing organization under a regime the 10-K describes as imposing significant costs and competitive burdens. That cost raises the bar for any new entrant, which would also need to draw liquidity away from established benchmarks. The same regulation can constrain CME, which the risk section takes up.

moatFactors.name: Capital-light economics
moatFactors.body: The model needs little capital, so most incremental revenue reaches cash. That lets CME fund technology and new products from a small share of cash flow and still pay most of it out, an advantage over any rival that must invest heavily to compete for the same liquidity.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat WIDE with high confidence. Liquidity and cross-margining reinforce each other, and the regulatory barrier sits on top of both. The limits on durability come from outside the competitive position: regulation that adds a transaction tax or requires more guaranty-fund capital could impair the economics, and volume rises and falls with market volatility however strong the moat is. Longer term, the open questions are new venues and products, the legal status of event contracts, and how the shift of infrastructure to Google Cloud performs. What the price assumes is not only that the moat holds, which we expect, but that volume keeps growing into it, and that part is cyclical.

points: Consensus sees FY26E revenue of about $7B (+8%) and EPS of $12.25, then FY27E revenue of $7.4B and EPS of $12.93, a slowdown to mid-single-digit growth in the second year. FY26E needs the second half to grow faster than the second quarter did, so the estimate leans on volume recovering rather than holding at second-quarter levels.
Market data is the steadiest growth line. It rose 18% in the first six months of 2026 even as trading volume softened in the second quarter, and the second-quarter gain was faster still.

Retail adoption of micro contracts cuts both ways. The company credits precious-metals micro contracts among its retail clients with sustaining metals volume, but micro contracts also lowered the average rate per contract, so volume growth from that source adds less revenue per contract.

New products are optional upside not yet in the figures: Single-Stock futures, 1-Ounce Gold contracts available 24/7, U.S. Treasury clearing, Compute futures, and sports-index futures with FutureSports. Event contracts carry legal uncertainty, which the 10-K says is the subject of litigation in various jurisdictions.

The move to Google Cloud is a cost question as much as a growth one: the company flags variable costs and duplicative on-premise and cloud costs during the transition, and the technology expense growth noted in the financials is the place it would show.

management.leadership: The March 2026 proxy names Terrence A. Duffy as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer and Lynne C. Fitzpatrick as President and Chief Financial Officer, with titles as of December 31, 2025; the July 22, 2026 earnings release still identifies Terry Duffy as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. The other named executive officers were Derek L. Sammann, Global Head of Commodities Markets, Julie M. Winkler, Chief Commercial Officer, and Sunil K. Cutinho, Chief Information Officer. On execution, the core business is run well: margins stayed high through a soft volume quarter. The weaker sign is cost growth outpacing revenue in the second quarter, and the initiatives management promotes, from new contracts to the cloud migration, are not yet visible in revenue. We weight the base business, which is strong, above the initiatives, which are unproven.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is simple: keep debt at a fixed level, spend little on capital projects, and pay out the rest through dividends and buybacks, as the cash-flow discussion details. For a business with this cash conversion and low leverage, that is the right default. The trade-off showed in the first half of 2026, when distributions ran ahead of earnings and the year-end cash pile was paid down to below the debt balance. That is not a strain at the current leverage, but it leaves less cushion if a low-volatility stretch lasts. The company's own list of risk factors includes its ability to continue to generate funds and manage its indebtedness, which is the right thing to monitor; nothing in the pack suggests it is under pressure.
management.governance: The governance view rests on the DEF 14A filed March 23, 2026. The board requires a majority of independent directors and fully independent audit, compensation, and nominating and governance committees, under categorical standards the company says conform to and exceed Nasdaq's. At the 2025 annual meeting approximately 87% of shareholders voted for the advisory resolution on executive pay. 2025 bonuses reflected cash earnings at about 114.3% of the target goal, performance shares from the September 2022 award vested at 200.0% of target in March 2026, and the September 2025 grants tie half of the performance shares to total shareholder return relative to the S&P 500 and half to absolute net income margin over 2026-2028. One feature is specific to CME: some directors are members of its exchanges, and members of CME can elect six directors. The nominating and governance committee reviews those directors' trading for independence. We see this as a structure shareholders should understand rather than a red flag. The chairman and chief executive roles are combined.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt in the pack covers board independence, the member-director election right and the compensation framework, but it does not quantify director or officer share ownership, so we assert no insider-ownership figure.

idiosyncratic: Volume dependence is the main risk and is already visible. Revenue follows volume, and volume follows market volatility; the second-quarter declines came, in the company's account, as volatility subsided from an elevated first quarter. A long low-volatility stretch would press on the core revenue line while costs keep rising, which is the Bear case.

The average rate per contract fell in the second quarter and the first half. The company attributes the drop largely to more micro-contract volume in equities, energy and metals and a higher share of member trading, partly offset by fee increases that took effect on April 1, 2026. If those mix shifts continue, revenue can fall even when volume holds.

One clearing firm accounted for at least 10% of clearing and transaction fees in the first six months of 2026. The company believes the customer portion of a departing firm's activity would likely move to another clearing firm, which is a reasonable view for a market where the liquidity sits with the exchange, but a firm's own trading would not necessarily follow.

Regulation is a standing risk. The 10-K flags possible transaction taxes, rules that could require more of the company's funds for the guaranty fund, and litigation over the legal status of event contracts. Heavy regulation also protects the franchise, so the exposure cuts both ways.

Clearing carries a tail risk. CME guarantees cleared contracts, and the company lists the ability of its credit and liquidity risk management to protect it from clearing-firm and counterparty credit risk, and to meet margin and liquidity needs in the BrokerTec matched principal business, among its risk factors. The probability is low but the severity would be high.
risks.systemic: CME's link to the market cycle is unusual. The 10-K notes that periods of heightened uncertainty have tended to increase trading volume through hedging and speculation, so a shock that hurts most companies can help CME, as the first quarter of 2026 showed. The relationship is not simple: the same filing warns that after a material market disturbance, extreme uncertainty may persist and reduce volume, and a long calm is plainly bad for the business. Interest rates matter in two ways. Uncertainty about Federal Reserve policy drives the interest-rate complex, which the company said softened in the second quarter as that uncertainty eased, and the company lists variances in earnings on the cash and collateral its clearing house holds as a factor in its results. Policy risk sits on top, through a possible transaction tax or a repeal of the 60/40 tax treatment of futures, and the cloud migration adds a dependence on third-party technology providers. Most of these exposures are stabilizing, and several cut both ways.

body: We rate CME Group HOLD with a $250-$300 target range. The scenarios give a weighted fair value of $280.25 against the $276.01 price, an expected upside of 1.5% and a bear-case downside of 16.7%. The franchise is of high quality: liquidity in benchmark contracts, cross-margined clearing and a regulated position support a wide moat, the operating margin is near 65% and capital needs are small. The corrected balance sheet does not change that. CME carries a steady $3.4B of debt, was a small net debtor in four of the last five year-ends and again at June 30, 2026, and its leverage is low at 0.3x net debt/EBITDA.

The HOLD comes from the price against the moment. The valuation already pays for the quality, the Street is split, and the second quarter showed volume, clearing fees and the rate per contract all softening as volatility eased, while consensus for FY26 still needs a second-half pickup. We set the Base on the Street's median target, a slight de-rating from today's forward multiple, and give the Bear more weight than the Bull because the second quarter resembles the Bear's starting point.

On the same scenarios, the page's math would derive BUY at or below the low end of our range and SELL at or above its top. Beyond price, we would turn more positive if volume and the rate per contract recover together and EPS runs ahead of the FY26E consensus. We would turn more cautious if third-quarter results extend the second quarter's declines, the rate per contract keeps falling despite the April fee increases, or a transaction tax or higher guaranty-fund requirement advances.
